text: Hey, everybody. Where do deity concepts come from?  You'll hear a lot of people say that they are
naive attempts to explain the unknown, they're  about death anxiety, or they're about control,
and while there is some truth to each of these,  they don't come close to telling the whole story
collectively, much less in isolation. And when  we hold up one of these as the essence of deity
concepts, we're being misleading and it's usually  because these ideas serve the interests of some
rhetorical goal or another associated with our own  identity politics. In short, deity concepts arise
and persevere as a result of the interactions  of (1) intuitive cognitive frameworks associated   with our hypersensitivity to the presence  of mental agents in the world around us,
(2) our intuitive teleological outlook, and (3)  group dynamics associated with social cohesion and
social mores in large societies. Now, I divide  these into individual and social/institutional
dimensions, and I'll talk about each as I describe  one way to put the data together regarding how
deity concepts arise and are transmitted.  But first I want to describe two important
theoretical models that undergird these data.  First, our cognition seems to sit on a spectrum
that runs from intuitive cognition that is rapid  and automatic and outside of our control—and
frequently our awareness—all the way to reflective  cognition that is slower, more intentional,
and based on things like reason and logic  and authority. So when I talk about intuitive   cognition, I'm talking about subconscious  cognitive frameworks that are shared universally,
or near universally, by humans because they have  been embedded in our cognitive architecture by   human evolution or by the universal experiences  of being human, such as our unilateral reliance
on other human agents to survive through infancy  or our need to be able to distinguish ourselves
from our environment and to detect the presence of  agents in the environment around us. So this leads
to the second theoretical model, which holds that  we do not passively experience the world around
us. Our minds mediate and project our experience  of the world, based not only on structuring the
stimuli and input that they receive but also on  anticipating and predicting what's coming next.
Dreams are one example of our minds projecting  those experiences from memories and expectations,   and optical illusions are one way to display
the way the mind's expectations  don't always align with the stimuli.   As an example, this image should look to you like  two objects of two different shades of gray, but
if you hold your finger up over the highlighted  and shadowed part where the two objects meet,   you should be able to see that they are the exact  same shade of gray. If that doesn't work, you may
need to obscure the shadows and the highlights  around the other edges. But the reason you see   two different shades of gray is that the image has  been crafted to convince your mind to interpret
this as a three-dimensional object in space. It  expects the light source to be coming from above
and therefore the object in the light to be a  lighter color than the object in the shadows.   Because they're the same shade of gray, your  intuitive cognition revises the experience
it projects so that you see the top object as  a darker gray and the bottom is a lighter gray.
This is your mind altering incoming data in  order to make it fit its expectations about   the world around it. So let's talk about  the individual dimension of deity concepts.
The conceptual foundation of deity concepts  is our hypersensitivity to the presence of   agency in the world around us, and this  is rooted deep in our evolutionary past.
The ability to detect the presence of agents in  their environment was critical to the survival   of our evolutionary predecessors. Those who  most quickly determined the rustling in the
bushes was an agent that might be focused on  them more regularly passed on their genes than
those who first assumed it was just the wind.  Now because of the comparatively low cost of
false positives to false negatives—maybe  you get laughed at versus you die—there
was no real ceiling to the effect of those  selection pressures, leaving modern humans
with a hair trigger to agency that can be  tripped by a variety of cues. If you've ever
seen a scary movie and then had trouble sleeping  that night because every time you closed your eyes   you got the distinct impression there was  something or someone in the room with you,
you've had experience with your mind projecting  the experience of the presence of an agent.

Another common manifestation of the perception of  presence has to do with deceased loved ones. After   years of being conditioned to the presence of  loved ones, our minds become sensitive to the cues
of their presence—their face, a smell, a piece of  jewelry or clothing—and our minds don't just turn
these cues off once that loved one passes away.  When those cues appear, the mind can project
the experience of their presence. For instance, I  have photos of a very good friend of mine who was
killed in a car accident about 20 years ago that  I may happen to look at every five years or so,
but each time I do, it floods my mind with  memories and with the sense of their presence.
Now imagine early societies tens of thousands of  years ago sharing stories around the fire about
experiencing the presence of deceased loved ones,  or generating and sharing ideas about agents
that might be causing certain events in  nature. So our teleological outlook is this
um assumption that things happen for a reason, and  so when things that we don't understand happen we
usually look for a cause, and intuitively an agent  is going to be the first place we look. Now, human
speech allows us to share these experiences and  these stories, which allows them to proliferate
and to be elaborated upon. Human imagination is  another important key to this because this is
what allows us to construct and communicate about  alternative realities, which are realities that
are not immediately accessible by our senses right  now. So, for instance, the concept of tomorrow
is an alternative reality. Stories about where  our deceased kin are and what they're doing
are intern—um, alternative realities. Institutions  like nations, like corporations, are alternative
realities. They do not exist in the world  of our senses, they're just social fictions
that we've agreed to share. What our deceased kin  are doing in this world of unseen agents that may
be creating changing or otherwise influencing our  world is another alternative reality, and when we   combine this feature of human imagination  with human speech and with the creation of
material media that allow us to exteriorize and  materialize these agents in their world—hybrid
animal-human creatures, for instance, represent  some of our earliest representative art that we've
ever found—we get increasingly complex alternative  realities that can be externally stored
and then incrementally elaborated on as  they get transmitted across social groups
and down through the generations. So this brings  us to the social and institutional dimension
Once we've created and shared unseen agents  like deceased kin or other entities that may   be out there influencing our world, and have  shared them with others in order for them to
be transmitted and passed down and to persevere,  we've got to agree on their nature and background.
And this is where social groups and institutions  come in. Not all individuals are going to agree
on an unseen agent concept, and so it will just  vanish once the creator or the primary cheerleader
of that particular agent is gone. So to survive  it needs to rise above the individual dimension
and become embedded within a broader social  framework like a social institution. So how
do we make a concept that may only intuitively  resonate with a few members of the social group
become attractive to all the members of a social  group? Some institution needs to find value
in enforcing a particular agent's profile,  and the majority of the group needs to find
value in adopting that profile. The dynamics that  achieve both of these ends the most successfully
are those associated with "prosociality," which  refers to forces that maintain social cohesion
as groups grow in size and complexity beyond the  prosocial capacities of frameworks like kinship.
Kinship is an evolutionary—evolutionarily  fundamental relationship that is very intuitive.
We naturally tend to treat members of our own  kinship network with more trust, even if we don't
really know them. There are obviously exceptions  to this, but by and large there is cooperation and
trust baked into kinship networks in a way that  is not found with other kinds of relationships.
If I live in a society that's large and complex  enough that my social success will frequently
require I engage with someone I have never seen  before who is not a member of my kinship network,
I need some other framework that's going to make  me feel comfortable putting my trust in them   and cooperating with them. With large and  advanced societies, language can frequently
fill that role. For instance, if I live in a  larger city, or by a larger city where they have   a certain accent or speak a certain language, but  I happen to engage in some kind of exchange with
someone whose accent or language more closely  matches my own, I may sense this person is a
part of my closer group over and against the more  distant and dominant group over there. I may feel
more trust intuitively. I may be more willing  to cooperate or even go out of my way to help
this stranger because of that framework. If  you've ever been traveling in a foreign country
and have come across someone whose language  or accent tells you they're from your homeland   or maybe even your hometown, maybe you've had  that experience of intuitively feeling relief
or comfort at someone who is situated at a much  smaller social distance from the other people   there you're more regularly interacting  with. I know I have had that experience.
Today we have large and complex constellations  of different social identities though,   so there may be a lot of different social bases  that need to be tagged before we decide we trust
someone in a situation like that. Anyway, another  framework for increasing cooperation and trust is
associated with a relationship with a specific  unseen agent. The ones that tend to become the
most socially widespread and salient are  those that can explain unknown phenomena,
can offer protection or aid in times of need  or crisis, can provide access to information
that helps us make decisions—think  prophecy, divination, necromancy—can
covertly monitor the social group, and  can punish violations of social standards,
such as free riding (which refers to enjoying  the benefits that social stability offers
while violating the standards that  achieve or maintain that stability).   So these agents tend to need things in return,  however, and so social groups must curate
interactions and exchanges with those agents.  This often takes the shape of ritual and of
standards of behavior. And while ritual is often  rationalized primarily as this locus of exchange
with the agent, rituals provide a benefit back  to the social group or the institution in the
form of prosociality. Rituals can be prosocial to  the degree that they produce a sense of solidarity
among members of a group or act as costly  signaling or credibility enhancing displays.
These are acts or behaviors that are considered  costly in terms of time, money, effort,
social standing, or even physical exertion or  pain. And so their fulfillment demonstrates to
others in a group that the person doing  them is willing to incur those costs   in order to achieve or maintain standing within  the group. They must be dedicated to the group
and its values and mores if they're willing to  incur those costs. The other behavioral standards
that often involve dress, diet, language, or  conventionalized social interactions help to
curate the relationship with the unseen agent  and help the social group to engage in boundary
maintenance and to again mitigate free-riding.  The more conspicuous or readily available this
signaling, the more it can facilitate trust among  members of a social group and tamp down free   riding and violations of the group's standards  as the group grows in size and complexity.
Many cognitive scientists of religion think  that the growth of early human societies   was facilitated in large part by the prosocial  forces offered by unseen agents like large-scale
socially concerned deities. Several  debates have been ongoing in this research,   however. One is the question of whether deity  concepts are an evolutionary adaptation or
are what's known as a spandrel or a side effect  of a separate evolutionary adaptation. I think
the best argument there is the hybrid  view that I've followed in this video   that sees the production of concepts of unseen  agents within the individual dimension as a
byproduct of our hypersensitivity to the  presence of agents in the world around us,
our capacity for imagination and speech, and so  forth, and sees the spread and perseverance of
those concepts within the social and institutional  dimension as an outcome of cultural evolution. The
deity concepts and their constituent features that  become the most widespread and salient tend to
be those that maximize the fitness of the social  group within its social and material environment.
Sometimes this has to do with cooperation,  other times it has to do with competition.   Let's consider one way this likely contributed  to deity concepts that are most widespread today.
Three of the most fundamental contributions of  deity concepts to prosociality are the ability to
provide full access to strategic information,  the ability to covertly monitor behavior,
and the ability to protect, punish, or offer aid  in time of need or crisis.So as deity concepts
compete, the ones that outperform others in  these regards tend to win out. People are
constantly asserting their deities are better  than the other city-states or nations deities.
Ours is more powerful. That was demonstrated  when we defeated you in battle, or when my
sick grandmother was healed of her illness. Our  deity knows more. That was demonstrated when they
instructed us when and what to plant this last  season, giving us the best harvest we've ever had,
or when they predicted a fire or an earthquake.  Ours monitors more and is more aware of what's
going on. That was demonstrated when a suspected  thief was convicted in an ordeal by the divine
image, or when they warned us of a a coup that  was being uh concocted. We see precisely this
kind of rhetoric in the Bible with the constant  one-upmanship and rhetoric of incomparability
compared to the other gods of the nations. For  instance, in Exodus, "Who is like you, O YHWH,
among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in  holiness, awesome in splendor, doing wonders?"
Isaiah 41:23 challenges the gods of the nations,  saying, "Make known what is coming after so that
we may know that you are gods. Do good or evil  so that we see and will be terrified together."
So after millennia of one-upmanship and then the  inclusion of philosophical rationalizing about the
ability of our deity to know more, to see more, to  do more, we arrive at the ultimate superlatives:
our deity is not just "more," they are "all."  They are omniscient, they are omnipresent,
and they are omnipotent. So these features of  contemporary "monotheistic" conceptualizations
of deity are superlative takes on precisely  those qualities of deity that increase their
fitness within social groups millennia ago.  Another debate within the cognitive science
of religion has to do with the precise cognitive  mechanisms involved in the production of these   concepts. On the individual level, some cognitive  scientists of religion suggest concepts that are
minimally counterintuitive tend to stand out  more. What minimal counter-intuitiveness refers
to is a degree of counterintuitiveness that  is high enough to make an agent stand out as
interesting and different, but not so high  as to make it nonsensical or unappealing.
I've not really adopted this framework in my own  work, just because the data can be a little mixed,
but I'm keeping my eye on on that debate.  Another big debate has to do with the
relationship of deity concepts to the rapid  growth of populations. Did socially concerned
deity concepts make that growth possible, or  did they develop in the wake of that growth?
This debate is also still ongoing and I'm  also just watching from the sidelines.   So if you're interested in learning more  about this research, there are a number of
wonderful books and papers out there on this  topic. I'll add some in the comments, but   two books in particular that I recommend are  Ilkka Pyyasiäinen's 2009 book, Supernatural
Agents, and Ara Norenzayan's 2013 book, Big Gods.  A number of scholars also published a wonderful
discussion in the journal Behavioral and Brain  Sciences a few years after Big Gods came out   that is freely available online and goes  into quite a bit of detail about these
debates. I'll link to that paper in the video  description. Hope that's given you something   to think about. I hope you all are having a  wonderful week, and I will see you around.
